title: The Trisynaptic Loop
excerpt: Perceiving and simulating worldly events is an "all hands" effort, drawing on hierarchical representations of spatiotemporal relationships among agents, objects, and environments; this results in interactions between otherwise isolated networks . EM network la
html:
Perceiving and simulating worldly events is an "all hands" effort, drawing on hierarchical representations of spatiotemporal relationships among agents, objects, and environments; this results in interactions between otherwise isolated networks 1.

EM network largely corresponds to the default mode network

Episodic memory is implemented by a cortico-hippocampal loop that takes richly structured input from the medial temporal cortex, performs aggressive sparsification and binding in the hippocampus, and broadcasts an indexed trace back to cortex and to control circuits. Within the hippocampus, information flows through a highly organized circuit known as the trisynaptic loop, which sequentially connects distinct subfields - the dentate gyrus, CA3, and CA1 - each performing specialized computations essential for episodic memory encoding and retrieval 2. Adult-born dentate-gyrus neurons participate in hippocampal circuit processing (Figure) 14. A contextual fear-conditioning paradigm follows memory from learning through later processing (Figure).

Hippocampal Circuitry and the Trisynaptic Loop

At the system level, the hippocampal formation is largely organized as a feedforward excitatory circuit. Unlike most cortical networks which are highly recurrent, the hippocampus routes information in a mostly unidirectional manner through its subfields 3.

Sensory inputs from multiple modalities are first processed in hierarchically organized cortical pathways and funneled into the entorhinal cortex (EC), specifically the superficial layers (II/III) of the EC 4. The entorhinal cortex serves as the gateway to the hippocampus: neurons in layer II of EC project via the perforant path to the dentate gyrus (and also to CA3), while layer III fibers (the temporoammonic pathway) project directly to CA1 and subiculum; deep EC (layer V/VI) receives hippocampal/subicular output, closing the loop. This layer-specific organization is conserved in humans and is measurably engaged in encoding versus retrieval, with superficial EC more active during encoding and deep EC during retrieval. These anatomy-function correspondences give the system two input routes-an indirect trisynaptic path EC->DG->CA3->CA1 optimized for separation/binding, and a monosynaptic EC->CA1 path optimized for fast comparison to current input 4, 5, 6. This recent study illustrates figure 1 (Figure). This recent study illustrates figure 2 (Figure).

Within the classical trisynaptic loop, the information flow is as follows: (1) Entorhinal layer II axons (perforant path) synapse onto dentate gyrus granule cells (first synapse); (2) Dentate granule cells activate CA3 pyramidal neurons via mossy fiber axons (second synapse); (3) CA3 pyramidal cells project to CA1 pyramidal neurons via the Schaffer collateral pathway (third synapse). CA1 in turn sends output to the subiculum and back to the deep layers of entorhinal cortex (which project out to neocortical association areas), effectively closing the loop; highly processed multimodal inputs from many cortical areas converge onto the hippocampus (especially into a single integrated network in CA3), and after hippocampal processing, the output diverges back to many cortical and subcortical targets via EC, subiculum, and fornix projections. Such architecture places the hippocampus in a pivotal position to bind distributed inputs into a unified memory trace (during encoding) and later reinstate or index that trace across the cortex (during recall) 7. Dentate Gyrus and Mossy Fiber Pathway: Encoding New Patterns

The dentate gyrus (DG) is the first processing stage in the trisynaptic loop and plays a critical role in encoding new episodic memory representations. Anatomically, the DG receives the bulk of cortical input to the hippocampus: entorhinal layer II perforant path fibers form synapses on the dendrites of dentate granule cells in the DG’s molecular layer. This is a densely convergent projection - in rodents, roughly a million granule cells receive projections from the EC. Only a small fraction of granule cells are active at any given time, however, reflecting extremely sparse coding in the DG. Such sparse activity (on the order of a few percent or less of neurons active in any environment) is a hallmark of the DG and is believed to underlie pattern separation - the process of orthogonalizing or decorrelating input patterns so that similar experiences are stored as distinct memories. This makes overlapping inputs (e.g. two similar contexts or events) produce more divergent neural representations, reducing interference between memories. Consistent with this idea, empirical studies have shown that small changes in input (for example, slight alterations in the environment) can lead to large changes in DG granule cell activation patterns, indicating separation of representations.

After processing by the DG, information is relayed to area CA3 via the mossy fibers, the axons of dentate granule cells. The mossy fiber (MF) pathway is distinctive in both its anatomy and function. Unlike the diffuse perforant path input, each granule cell makes only a few, but extremely powerful, synapses onto CA3 pyramidal neurons. In the rat, a single CA3 cell receives on the order of  40-50 mossy fiber contacts (out of hundreds of thousands of granule cells) 7, yet each individual mossy fiber synapse is giant and efficacious. These synapses have been termed "detonator synapses" because a single presynaptic burst can reliably trigger a postsynaptic spike in CA3 8. Indeed, mossy terminals form multiple active zones and release a large glutamate volume, producing an unusually large excitatory postsynaptic potential in CA3. Moreover, short-term plasticity at the mossy synapse is dominated by frequency facilitation: repetitive spikes from a granule cell lead to progressively larger transmitter release, enhancing the postsynaptic impact by up to  1200% during theta-frequency bursts 3. In practice, this means that isolated DG spikes have relatively little effect on CA3, but if a granule cell fires a high-frequency burst (as might happen when a salient or novel input strongly drives the DG), the later spikes in the burst can "ignite" the CA3 neuron. This conditional high-pass filter property prevents CA3 from being overactivated by noise or minor cues, while ensuring that a strongly activated DG cell (or small set of cells) can rapidly trigger a new memory engram in CA3. Functionally, the sparse and strong DG->CA3 connections impose a form of random orthogonalization: by connecting to only a random tiny subset of CA3 cells, each active granule cell helps produce a new, largely uncorrelated pattern of CA3 activity (compared to other memories). This randomness, combined with DG’s sparse coding, is thought to maximize the ability of CA3 to encode many distinct memories with minimal overlap 9.

Biologically, the DG has several special features that support these functions. In addition to its sparse activity, the DG is one of the few brain regions with adult neurogenesis - new granule cells are generated throughout life. Newborn granule cells are highly excitable and plastic, which some theories suggest may contribute to pattern separation by introducing more variability and flexibility in encoding new memories (e.g. new neurons can rapidly integrate into circuits and potentially encode subtle differences in experiences). The DG also contains feedforward inhibitory circuits (via interneurons in the hilus) that tightly control when and which granule cells fire, preventing runaway excitation and further decorrelating inputs 3.

CA3 Recurrent Network: Autoassociation and Pattern Completion

Area CA3 lies at the heart of the hippocampal memory system. It is often described as an autoassociative network or attractor network because of the extensive recurrent connections between its pyramidal neurons 9. In CA3, each pyramidal cell not only receives feedforward input from DG (mossy fibers) and EC (perforant path), but also sends out collateral axons that synapse on other CA3 cells. Anatomically, this recurrent collateral system is remarkably well-developed: in the rodent CA3 there are on the order of 300,000 pyramidal cells, and each one makes recurrent synapses onto thousands of other CA3 cells. Estimates suggest  12,000 recurrent synapses per CA3 neuron in rats, implying a  2-4% probability of connection between any two CA3 neurons (with near-complete connectivity when considering the network as a whole). These recurrent projections span the entire CA3 region (not just locally), effectively linking all CA3 neurons into one integrated network. By comparison, estimates indicate that each human CA3 subregion contains on the order of 1.7 million pyramidal neurons, reflecting a substantial scaling-up relative to the roughly 300,000 neurons observed in rodents 10. Such widespread recurrent coupling means that once a subset of CA3 neurons is activated (by an input or cue), they can excite each other in a positive feedback loop, tending to drive the entire network into a coherent activation pattern.

The computational significance of the CA3 recurrent network is profound. It provides the substrate for rapid one-shot learning and pattern completion in episodic memory. Because CA3 plasticity is strong and rapid (in part due to NMDA receptor-rich synapses), even a single exposure can "wire together" the active neurons, fulfilling the need for one-trial episodic learning. Later, if a partial or degraded cue of that event is received (for instance, only some elements of the original experience are present), the recurrent CA3 network can complete the pattern: the subset of neurons activated by the cue will reactivate their interconnected partners, reconstructing the full original activity pattern representing the entire memory (a hallmark of episodic recall). Studies have shown that disrupting CA3 (or blocking CA3-specific NMDA receptors required for plasticity) impairs the ability to recall memories from partial cues, confirming that CA3’s recurrent synapses are critical for pattern completion in vivo 7.

Importantly, the CA3 network does not act in isolation; it operates in concert with the feedforward inputs. The dentate gyrus and mossy fibers provide what could be called the "encoding drive," while the entorhinal cortex perforant path provides context and cues for retrieval. Theoretical models (e.g. by Treves & Rolls) posit a division of labor: During learning, the sparse but extremely strong mossy fiber inputs from DG dominate CA3 activity - effectively "forcing" a new pattern to be stored in the recurrent synapses regardless of prior activity. During retrieval, however, the direct perforant path input from EC (which is much more numerous in synapse count, though individually weaker) serves as the initial cue to trigger recall. Even a partial cue coming from EC can activate some of the originally stored CA3 cells, and then the recurrent collaterals take over to complete the full pattern of activation. In this way, the system uses EC inputs to probe CA3 for a stored memory, and CA3’s autoassociation to reignite the full memory. Consistent with this, experimental lesions have shown that disrupting the perforant path input to CA3 impairs memory retrieval, whereas blocking the mossy fiber input impairs new learning but not recall 7. From another perspective, CA3’s recurrent network also endows it with capacity for temporally extended representations. Episodic memories often involve sequences of events unfolding over time, and CA3 is thought to link events across temporal gaps. The attractor dynamics, with inherent reverberatory activity, can maintain a memory active for a short period and form associations not just in space (what happened where) but also in time (what happened when/in what order). Modeling and recordings have suggested that CA3 neurons can encode sequential relationships (e.g. "time cells" that fire at specific moments in a temporally structured experience), supporting memory for the flow of events 11. In short, CA3 provides the associative glue for the episodic memory system, rapidly binding together the who/what/where/when of an episode into a single representation, and allowing that representation to be stored, maintained, and completed when needed.

CA1 and Output Pathways: Integration, Sequence Ordering, and Memory Retrieval

The final relay in the trisynaptic loop is area CA1, which performs an integrative role and serves as the primary output node (together with subiculum) from the hippocampus. CA1 pyramidal neurons receive a dual input: one set of excitatory inputs comes from CA3 (the Schaffer collateral synapses), and another comes directly from entorhinal cortex layerIII (the temporoammonic pathway). These two inputs carry somewhat different information - the CA3 input conveys the outcome of hippocampal processing (pattern-completed representations, sequences generated internally, etc.), while the direct EC input carries current cortical activity (often reflecting the external sensory context or ongoing experience). By combining these, CA1 is thought to act as a comparator or associator that checks whether the hippocampus’s reconstruction (from CA3) matches the current input from the environment. If there is a mismatch (for example, the expected pattern from CA3 doesn’t align with what EC is signaling), CA1 neurons can detect this novelty or discrepancy - essentially flagging that the current situation does not match a known memory. This mismatch detection function of CA1 has been hypothesized in several models 12, 13 and is supported by evidence that CA1 is particularly sensitive to changes in input patterns and can signal prediction errors (a critical component for learning when an outcome is unexpected). Thus, CA1 may contribute to episodic memory by ensuring that retrieved memories are compared against reality, and by driving learning of new representations when mismatches occur. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure). The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Beyond novelty detection, CA1 also temporally refines and outputs the hippocampal code. Some theories propose that CA1 "orders" or sequences the information it receives from CA3, helping to organize the elements of an episode in time. In rodent studies, CA1 place cells and time cells can represent sequences of locations or temporal intervals, respectively, and CA1 is known to exhibit sharply timed firing relative to network oscillations (like theta phase precession) which could underpin a timeline for events. By receiving input from CA3 (which may contain partially formed sequences) and the EC (current context), CA1 might align these inputs to produce a coherent spatio-temporal representation - essentially a timeline of events within a context 2.

Anatomically, CA1 pyramidal neurons project to the subiculum and back to the deep layers of the entorhinal cortex (layers V/VI). From entorhinal deep layers, the information is sent out to various cortical areas (including the parahippocampal and perirhinal cortices and then to widespread association cortices) as well as other targets such as the medial prefrontal cortex. In this way, CA1/subiculum serve as the main output relay of the hippocampus, communicating the result of hippocampal processing (e.g. a retrieved memory or a newly encoded pattern) back to the rest of the brain. This hippocampal-neocortical feedback is essential for memory retrieval: it allows a reactivated hippocampal memory to reinstate the corresponding pattern of cortical activity that represents the details of the episode (often referred to as the hippocampus acting as an index to retrieve distributed cortical engrams). Over time (during systems consolidation), repeated reactivation via these outputs may strengthen direct connections among cortical areas so that the memory becomes gradually less hippocampus-dependent (and more abstract/generalized).

Putting this together, the episodic system is a set of coupled modules with complementary inductive biases: EC supplies structured coordinates over items, contexts, and experienced time; DG generates ultra-sparse, interference-resistant patterns; CA3 stores and completes indices with attractor dynamics; CA1 computes prediction error and orchestrates retrieval versus updating; subiculum/EC and thalamo-prefrontal loops distribute and regulate the trace.
